PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let me walk you through what September is telling us about your SiteTransformer at ARMI Manufacturing — and why this field deserves attention now rather than later. Your transformer is a 500 kVA unit, and it's running without reactive compensation. The field is registering an 89.2 percent power factor — which sounds reasonable until you understand what that 10.8-point gap is costing you. The daily supply target is anchored at 248 kilovolt-amperes, and during weekday production, roughly 80 to 85 percent of your active production intervals are running at or above that ceiling. The transformer is doing the work — but it's doing it the hard way. On the voltage side, your field is averaging 493 volts against a 480-volt nominal reference. That's 13 volts of chronic overvoltage, sustained across the entire production month. And it's not smooth — the field is swinging between a high of 502 and a low of 483.9 volts. That's an 18-volt range, with the low end sitting less than 4 volts above your nominal floor. Your motors and drives are getting overvoltage most of the time, then absorbing periodic sag pulses during shift starts and large motor inrush events. That combination is the most accelerating thermal and insulation-aging scenario you can run electrical equipment through. The reactive burden is 29.2 kilovolt-amperes reactive on average, spiking to 58.1 at peak. And there's a moment in September — visible in the active-reactive view — where the power factor dropped all the way down to 62.7 percent. That's the field at its worst: carrying nearly as much reactive current as active, productive current. That's waste. That's heat. That's cost. The monthly consequence total from the baseline view: roughly $358 per month, or approximately $4,357 per year. That's the financial expression of what this untuned field is generating in energy waste, thermal burden, and cooling overhead every production cycle. MPTS correction projects a 99.5 percent power factor, recovering an estimated $285 per month — approximately $3,472 per year — with released capacity returned to the transformer's usable headroom. That's a meaningful recovery on a field that's ready for it. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
Here's the executive summary on SiteTransformer at ARMI Manufacturing for September 2026. The field is untuned. Power factor is at 89.2 percent, reactive burden peaks at 58.1 kilovolt-amperes reactive, and the transformer is exceeding its 248 kilovolt-ampere daily supply target during roughly 80 to 85 percent of active production intervals. The monthly consequence cost is an estimated $358 per month — approximately $4,357 per year — in energy waste, thermal burden, and cooling overhead. The voltage field is running chronically elevated at 493 volts average against a 480-volt nominal, with an 18-volt swing range and recurring demand-sag dips on shift starts. The harmonic profile includes a maximum iTHD of 24.4 percent and a minimum power factor excursion to 62.7 percent — both stress events worth monitoring. MPTS simulation projects a 99.5 percent power factor recovery, dropping reactive burden from 58.1 to 30.3 kilovolt-amperes reactive maximum, and recovering an estimated $3,472 per year in field consequence costs. Recommended next steps are reactive compensation scoping, a harmonic characterization study, and a transformer thermal baseline inspection. All financial figures are planning-level estimates. ---

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me give you the complete engineering picture on SiteTransformer at ARMI Manufacturing — walking through the voltage, the reactive burden, the harmonics, and what the MPTS simulation is showing us for September 2026. Start with the voltage field, because it sets the context for everything else. Your average operating voltage for September is 493.1 volts — and your nominal reference is 480 volts line-to-line. That's 13 volts of sustained overvoltage across an entire production month. Now, 13 volts over nominal doesn't sound dramatic — but when every motor winding, every drive input stage, and every transformer core in your facility is absorbing that excess voltage continuously, the cumulative insulation aging and thermal cycling stress becomes very real, very fast. What makes it more complex is the swing. The voltage field is moving between a high of 502 volts and a low of 483.9 volts — an 18-volt range. That lower boundary at 483.9 is less than 4 volts above your nominal floor. So you're simultaneously dealing with a chronically elevated average and a lower-boundary floor that's barely above nominal. The pattern driving those lows is visible in the voltage trace: recurring triangular dip signatures, clustered especially in the first ten days of September and repeating throughout the month. Those are shift-start inrush events — large motors coming online and pulling voltage down across the distribution system. They're not tripping protection, but they're creating repeated sag pulses that compound the already-elevated thermal stress environment. Device health risk assessment: moderate, trending toward elevated. The compounding of chronic overvoltage plus recurring sag dips is the most accelerating scenario for motor winding insulation degradation and VFD input capacitor stress. Now the reactive and harmonic layer. The baseline power factor is 89.2 percent — that means roughly 10.8 percent of every ampere flowing through this transformer is reactive current doing no productive work. The reactive average is 29.2 kilovolt-amperes reactive, and it peaks at 58.1 kilovolt-amperes reactive during production demand spikes. That nearly 2:1 peak-to-average ratio tells you the reactive burden isn't just a steady background cost — it surges dramatically when production loads engage, creating the highest thermal stress events at the moments when the transformer is already working hardest. The active-reactive-harmonic view adds two critical data points. First: the iTHD maximum of 24.4 percent. Your average harmonic distortion is a benign 1.7 percent — but that maximum represents a transient distortion event significant enough to cause real field disruption. At 24.4 percent iTHD, you're looking at harmonic current magnitudes that increase transformer core losses, heat neutral conductors, and can interfere with sensitive instrumentation and control systems. The purple harmonics trace running persistently throughout the month — even at low load — confirms that harmonic-generating loads like variable frequency drives or rectifiers are energized continuously on this transformer. Second: the minimum power factor excursion to 62.7 percent. That's the field at its absolute worst in September. At 62.7 percent power factor, the reactive current component is approximately 78 percent of the magnitude of the active current component. The transformer is carrying substantially more current than the productive work requires during that event. That's the moment of maximum thermal stress, maximum conductor heating, and maximum reactive loss — all happening simultaneously. The monthly consequence total from the baseline header: approximately $348 in energy waste consequence, $8 in thermal burden consequence, and $3 in cooling overhead consequence — totaling roughly $358 per month and approximately $4,357 per year. And 80 to 85 percent of your active weekday production intervals are running above the 248 kilovolt-ampere daily supply ceiling, meaning this stress pattern is not occasional — it's the operating norm. The MPTS simulation resolves most of this. With a 99.5 percent target power factor applied, the reactive average drops from 29.2 kilovolt-amperes reactive down to 9.2 — a 68 percent reduction in average reactive burden. The reactive maximum compresses from 58.1 down to 30.3 kilovolt-amperes reactive — reducing the worst-case current amplitude

SITETRANSFORMER.voltage_stability_findings:
**SiteTransformer Voltage Health — September 2026**

The voltage field on SiteTransformer tells an interesting story — elevated, cycling, and moderately stressed. The average operating voltage for September registers at 493.1 volts against a 480-volt line-to-line nominal reference. That 13-volt chronic elevation above nominal means every motor, drive, and control device connected to this transformer is living in a mild but continuous overvoltage condition for the majority of the production month.

The swing range adds another layer of concern. With a peak voltage of 502 volts and a minimum operating floor of 483.9 volts, the field is cycling across roughly an 18-volt window throughout the month. The minimum of 483.9 volts holds just barely above the 480-volt nominal floor — a margin of less than 4 volts — which means demand-driven sag events are reliably pushing the field toward the lower boundary even as the average rides elevated. That's the compounding stress dynamic: devices are getting chronic overvoltage on the high side, then periodic sag pulses on the low side, and the combination is the most damaging thermal and insulation-aging scenario you can run an industrial electrical system through.

The triangular voltage-drop patterns visible in the V trace are rhythmic and clustered, particularly dense in the first ten days of September, and continuing at regular frequency through the remainder of the month. This is consistent with production shift startups and large motor inrush events pulling voltage down on a repeating cycle. The dips are moderate in depth — not tripping protection systems — but frequent enough that their cumulative stress on motor windings, VFD input stages, and transformer core laminations is real and measurable over time.

Overall voltage health on SiteTransformer: **moderate risk**, trending toward elevated if this pattern persists without field correction. The chronic overvoltage average combined with recurring sag dips is the signature of a field that would benefit significantly from reactive compensation stabilizing the delivery voltage and reducing demand-driven voltage excursions.

---
SITETRANSFORMER.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**SiteTransformer Reactive and Harmonic Profile — September 2026**

The M view on SiteTransformer confirms what the BT header numbers suggest: this field is carrying a meaningful reactive burden that is present throughout production hours and punctuated by stress events that exceed the average by a notable margin.

Starting with the reactive picture: the baseline reactive average is 29.2 kVAR, and the reactive maximum reaches 58.1 kVAR. That's a peak-to-average ratio of nearly 2:1 — meaning when production demand spikes, the reactive burden roughly doubles from its steady-state level. The red amperage trace in the M view confirms this, regularly reaching the maximum amperage callout of 293.7 amps during production peaks. That current amplitude is what's driving thermal load into the transformer windings and the distribution conductors running through this facility.

The harmonic profile adds another dimension of stress. The average iTHD of 1.7 percent is benign on its own — but the maximum iTHD callout of 24.4 percent is the number that matters here. That peak harmonic event represents a transient distortion level that is significant enough to cause real field disruption. Harmonic currents at that magnitude increase transformer core losses, create neutral conductor heating in three-phase systems, and can interfere with sensitive control and metering equipment. The fact that the purple harmonics trace never disappears entirely — maintaining a persistent low-level presence even during reduced-load periods — tells you harmonic-generating loads are always energized on this transformer. VFDs, rectifiers, or switching power supplies are running continuously, not just during peak production.

The minimum power factor excursion visible in the M view at 62.7 percent is the single most concerning data point in the reactive profile. That's a severe lagging event — the field dropped more than 26 points below the already-suboptimal average power factor during at least one production event in September. At 62.7 percent power factor, the reactive current component is nearly as large as the active current component, meaning the transformer and associated conductors are carrying substantially more current than the actual productive work being done would require. That event, and any similar events that may not be captured in a single-month summary, represents the upper boundary of stress the transformer is experiencing.

---
SITETRANSFORMER.operational_stress_interpretation:
**SiteTransformer Operational Stress Assessment — September 2026**

Pulling the four views together into a coherent operational picture: SiteTransformer at ARMI Manufacturing is running a structured five-day production schedule with clear weekend load reduction, which is the expected and manageable pattern for an industrial manufacturing facility. The challenge isn't the production pattern itself — it's what the transformer is being asked to absorb every time that production load engages.

Every weekday production startup, the transformer field does three things simultaneously: it absorbs the inrush current from motor startups that creates those recurring triangular voltage dip signatures in the V view, it begins carrying the reactive burden that pushes the BT power factor below 90 percent, and it begins accumulating the thermal burden that converts wasted reactive power into heat dissipating from the transformer core and windings. Those three phenomena aren't independent — they're additive. The reactive burden increases apparent current through the transformer, which increases I-squared-R losses, which increases heat generation, which accelerates winding insulation aging and reduces transformer service life.

The monthly consequence totals from the BT header make this concrete: approximately $348 per month in energy waste consequence, $8 per month in thermal burden consequence, and $3 per month in cooling cost consequence — totaling roughly $358 per month and approximately $4,357 per year. Those numbers represent the measurable financial expression of the reactive and harmonic stress the field is accumulating every production month.

The 80 to 85 percent rate at which active production blocks breach the 248 kVA daily target means the transformer is operating above its comfort ceiling for the substantial majority of its working life. Over time, that consistent above-target operation, combined with the voltage swing stress and the reactive burden, creates a compounding degradation trajectory. The field is not in immediate distress — no outage events were detected, the voltage minimum holds above nominal — but the trajectory without correction points toward accelerating asset wear and growing consequence costs month over month.

The iTHD maximum of 24.4 percent and the minimum power factor excursion to 62.7 percent are the stress peaks to monitor. Those events, while not constant, represent the moments when the field is most vulnerable to cascading stress — drive faults, protection trips, or accelerated thermal damage in the transformer core.

---
SITETRANSFORMER.simulated_mpts_outcome:
**SiteTransformer — MPTS Simulation Results (S View) | September 2026**

The S view delivers the quantified projection of what reactive compensation does to this field — and the results are substantial. With MPTS correction applied, the simulated field achieves a 99.5 percent power factor target, representing a gain of 10.3 percentage points from the untuned baseline of 89.2 percent. That improvement is not cosmetic — it reshapes every aspect of how the transformer operates during production hours.

The reactive burden tells the clearest story. The reactive average drops from 29.2 kVAR down to 9.2 kVAR — a reduction of 20 kVAR, or roughly 68 percent of the average reactive burden disappearing from the field. The reactive maximum compresses from 58.1 kVAR down to 30.3 kVAR — a reduction of 27.8 kVAR at the peak stress level. That peak reduction is particularly meaningful because it directly reduces the worst-case current amplitude the transformer must carry during production demand spikes, which are exactly the moments when thermal stress is most intense.

The heat burden relief follows directly. With reactive current substantially reduced, the I-squared-R losses in the transformer windings and distribution conductors drop proportionally. The thermal consequence line in the S header reflects this — thermal burden contribution moving from $8 per month toward a significantly reduced figure. Cooling overhead similarly compresses. The facility's mechanical cooling systems — whether that's chilled air, HVAC, or process cooling — carry a lighter burden when the heat generation from wasted reactive power is reduced at the source.

Released capacity adds a practical operational benefit: 3.6 kVA of apparent power burden is returned to the transformer's usable capacity. That's headroom the facility can use for future load additions without immediately stressing the transformer beyond its comfort ceiling — relevant for any facility with growth plans or equipment upgrade schedules.

The aggregate financial projection: approximately $285 per month in recovered value, building to an estimated $3,472 per year in recovered consequence costs. The multi-year accumulation is meaningful — approximately $17,372 over five years, roughly $34,786 over ten years, and approaching $69,708 over a twenty-year planning horizon. All figures are planning-level estimates dependent on actual field conditions and site-specific factors.

The sizing implication from the kVAR MAX figure: 58.1 kVAR MAX ÷ 400 = 0.145, rounding up to one H490 unit. At this reactive load level, a single H490 unit — rated at 400 kVAR — provides substantial oversizing relative to the 58.1 kVAR maximum, which suggests that either an H240 unit at 200 kVAR nominal capacity may be sufficient for this specific transformer, or that a shared compensation strategy with other transformers on the site could optimize the investment. Final sizing should be confirmed through full engineering assessment once CSV data is available.

---
SITETRANSFORMER.recommended_engineering_attention_areas:
**SiteTransformer — Engineering Attention Areas | September 2026**

Given that this is an untuned field with no installed MPTS assets currently documented for SiteTransformer, the following attention areas are recommended as priorities for engineering review and remediation planning.

**First: Reactive compensation scoping.** The 58.1 kVAR maximum and 89.2 percent baseline power factor establish a clear reactive correction need. An H240 unit at 200 kVAR nominal should be assessed as a right-sized first option for this transformer given the relatively modest reactive peak. If site-wide aggregation of reactive demand across multiple transformers supports a larger shared asset, that architecture should be evaluated. Engineering scope and final installed cost estimates will depend on available panel space, conduit routing, and control integration requirements.

**Second: Harmonic characterization study.** The 24.4 percent iTHD maximum is a transient stress peak that warrants further investigation. A dedicated harmonic survey during a peak production shift would establish whether the harmonic source is a specific drive, rectifier bank, or combination of loads — and whether passive or active harmonic filtering is warranted in addition to reactive compensation. Without that characterization, there's residual uncertainty about whether reactive compensation alone fully addresses the peak stress events.

**Third: Voltage monitoring continuity.** The 493.1-volt average and 18-volt swing range should be tracked monthly to establish a trend baseline. If the average continues to creep upward or the swing range widens, that's an early indicator of field degradation that warrants transformer tap adjustment or upstream voltage regulation review.

**Fourth: Transformer thermal baseline.** Given the consistent above-target loading at 80 to 85 percent of production intervals exceeding 248 kVA, a thermal imaging inspection of the transformer enclosure and secondary conductors is advisable to establish a current condition baseline before reactive compensation is introduced.
